answer.question: What was the Kubernetes release cadence before 2021?
answer.answer: Historically, Kubernetes had a cadence of four releases per calendar year, roughly one per quarter. In 2020 that broke down. SIG Release extended the 1.19 cycle because of the COVID-19 pandemic, so 2020 ended up with only three minor releases, with 1.20 as the third and last. The KEP describes this as Kubernetes effectively moving to three releases per year in 2020. The formal change from four to three releases per year was only made official when the KEP merged on April 23, 2021, starting with the 1.22 release.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes moved from four releases a year (one per quarter) to three, effective from April 23, 2021, when the Release Team merged KEP-2572. The evidence gives several reasons:

- **Growing burden of releases:** As the project matured, each cycle carried more enhancements. That put more load on contributors and the Release Engineering team. It also made it harder for downstream consumers and integrators to keep up with ever more feature-packed releases. Wider adoption meant the complexity of supporting a fast-moving platform reached a bigger chain of consumers.
- **End users couldn't keep pace:** Most organizations could not do a minor version upgrade every 3 months, or would fall out of security support within a year. More frequent releases only reduce churn and risk if users can actually apply the upgrades. With fewer releases, users should spend less time upgrading and more time supporting their clusters.
- **Longer support:** Each minor version is supported somewhat longer, so bug fixes and security patches stay available longer. The blog notes this is not strictly an LTS policy.
- **More time for contributors:** Contributors get more time to mature enhancements and get them production-ready.
- **Less overhead for SIG Release:** Management overhead drops, and there are only 3 patch release branches to maintain instead of up to 4 overlapping. This leaves more time for release quality and tooling, for smoother handoffs between release teams, and possibly for more shadows.
- **Better planning and lower risk:** The schedule becomes more predictable and deterministic. There is more room for triage, development, conferences and cycle preparation.
- **COVID-19 context:** The 1.19 cycle had been extended to ease the burden on contributors and users during the pandemic, making 1.20 the third and final release of 2020. The 1.22 changelog says the release team was affected by the pandemic and listened to its user base about the number of releases per year.

The trade-off is a slower rate of feature graduation (alpha to stable going from about 9 to about 12 months), and each release will contain more enhancements.

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes enforces the Pod Security Standards in-tree with a built-in admission controller called Pod Security (the PodSecurity admission controller). It intercepts requests in the API server before they are stored and admits or denies them. Pod specs are checked against the configured Pod Security Standard, and the restrictions apply at the namespace level when pods are created. You can configure cluster-wide defaults and exemptions.

It has been built in since v1.22, where it was alpha and you had to enable the PodSecurity feature gate. It went beta in v1.23 and stable in v1.25. It is meant to replace the deprecated PodSecurityPolicies. It can also run as a standalone webhook instead of in-tree.

answer.question: What did Pod Security Admission replace, and when was that removed?
answer.answer: Pod Security Admission replaced PodSecurityPolicy (PSP). PSP was deprecated in Kubernetes v1.21 and removed in v1.25, and it no longer functions in v1.25 and later. In the same v1.25 release, Pod Security Admission graduated to stable. The stated reason for the removal was that the changes needed to make PSP easier to use would have been breaking changes, so it was removed in favor of a friendlier replacement.

answer.question: What were Pod Security Admission's graduation stages?
answer.answer:
Pod Security Admission (controlled by the `PodSecurity` feature gate) went through three stages:

- **Alpha in v1.22.** The gate was off by default, and so was the built-in admission controller. An initial set of E2E feature tests ran in an alpha test job. The alpha was released on 2021-08-04.
- **Beta in v1.23–1.24.** The gate was on by default and the admission plugin joined the default enabled set, though enforcement stayed opt-in per namespace. The beta criteria were:
  - support for the restricted policy on Windows pods
  - a deprecation/removal policy for old profile versions
  - support for ephemeral containers
  - a migration workflow from PodSecurityPolicy
  - re-assessing the API decisions from alpha feedback
  - closing test-coverage gaps

  The beta was released on 2021-11-03.
- **GA (stable) in v1.25.** The gate stayed on by default. The `pod-security.admission.config.k8s.io/v1` admission configuration API was added, unchanged from `v1beta1`. Several user-experience improvements were made, and conformance tests were to use the most restrictive level possible, though Pod Security Admission itself is not required for conformance. An earlier draft had aimed for GA in v1.24, ahead of PodSecurityPolicy's removal in v1.25.

The feature gate itself was listed as stable through v1.27 and was later removed.

answer.question: What happens to unused auto-generated ServiceAccount token Secrets?
answer.answer:
Starting in version 1.29, the legacy ServiceAccount token cleaner deals with them. It runs in kube-controller-manager and checks every 24 hours.

A Secret is marked invalid only if all of these are true:
- It is auto-generated, meaning a ServiceAccount references it in both directions.
- No pod currently mounts it.
- It has not been used for a set period since it was created or last used. The period defaults to one year.

The cleaner first checks the tracking ConfigMap, which exists if LegacyServiceAccountTokenTracking is enabled. It only proceeds once the set period has passed since the date in that ConfigMap. If the ConfigMap is unavailable, no Secrets are removed.

To mark a Secret invalid, the cleaner adds the label `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-invalid-since` with the current date as its value.

If someone uses an invalidated token, the validator:
- adds the audit annotation `authentication.k8s.io/legacy-token-invalidated: <secret name>/<namespace>`,
- increments the `invalid_legacy_auto_token_uses_total` metric,
- updates the `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used` label with the new date,
- returns an error saying the token has been invalidated.

Users can temporarily re-enable the token by removing the `invalid-since` label, or they can switch to the TokenRequest API.

If an invalid Secret stays unused for a further period (one year by default), the control plane deletes it. Administrators set both periods with the kube-controller-manager flag `--legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period`.

In earlier beta designs of the KEP (around releases 1.23–1.28), unused Secrets were to be deleted directly after the period, without being marked invalid first.

answer.question: Did Kubernetes create a token Secret for every ServiceAccount?
answer.answer:
Yes, but only before version 1.24. Up to then, Kubernetes automatically generated a Secret-based token for each ServiceAccount. In 1.24 the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` feature gate went to beta and was enabled by default. With it on, the token controller stops auto-creating these Secrets for every ServiceAccount.

Instead you get tokens through the TokenRequest API. If you need a non-expiring token, you can still create a Secret yourself, and the token controller fills it in with a service account token.

A ServiceAccount's `secrets` field tells the two kinds apart. A Secret referenced there counts as an auto-generated legacy token; one that isn't counts as manually created. From 1.29, auto-generated legacy tokens that go unused for a period (one year by default) are marked invalid. If they stay unused for that period again, the control plane purges them.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer: Because BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume went GA in 1.22, Pods now get their service account tokens through the TokenRequest API and store them in a projected volume. That made auto-generating Secret-based tokens unnecessary. The KEP also notes that these Secret-based tokens are less secure than bound tokens, which are time-limited and bound to specific Pods. The 1.29 release post describes the related cleanup work as a way to reduce potential attack surface. The LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature gate went beta, enabled by default, in 1.24 and stable in 1.26. Users were pointed to the TokenRequest API instead, or to a manually created Secret if a non-expiring token is needed.

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer:
It depends on the release. As of 1.36 and still current, yes: the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate is beta and enabled by default. With it on, built-in API fields reject IPv4 addresses with leading "0"s in any octet, CIDR values containing such IPs, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses such as ::ffff:192.168.0.1.

In 1.33–1.35 the answer is no. The gate was alpha and off by default, so such values were still accepted, and the API server returned a warning that they will be rejected in the future. Back in 1.23, Kubernetes deliberately kept allowing leading zeros, and interpreted them as decimal, to preserve compatibility.

The stricter validation covers only fields in built-in API kinds. It does not cover custom resource kinds, values in Kubernetes configuration files, or command-line arguments.

answer.question: Before strict IP validation was on by default, what happened when a Service used an IPv4 address with leading zeros?
answer.answer:
The value was accepted rather than rejected. Kubernetes deliberately kept allowing leading zeros in IPv4 addresses for compatibility. It parsed them as decimal by simply ignoring the extra zeros, so "012.000.001.002" became 12.0.1.2. Most libc-based code would instead treat those octets as octal (10.0.1.2), which is the mismatch behind CVE-2021-29923.

Instead of an error, the API server returned a warning saying the non-standard IP will be considered invalid in a future Kubernetes release and suggesting the canonical form, for example "use \"5.6.7.8\"". Service IP/CIDR fields have had these warnings since 1.27.

The StrictIPCIDRValidation gate was alpha and off by default from 1.33 to 1.35. With it disabled, an invalid Service .spec.clusterIP was still allowed, with a warning. It became beta and on by default in 1.36, after which such values are rejected.

answer.question: What are the release stages of strict IP/CIDR validation (KEP-4858)?
answer.answer:
Strict IP/CIDR validation is controlled by the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate. Its stages are:

- **Alpha:** Kubernetes 1.33 through 1.35, disabled by default.
- **Beta:** from Kubernetes 1.36, enabled by default.

The current feature gate reference lists no GA stage. However, the latest KEP-4858 document (valid from 1.37) claims status implemented/stable, and its outline includes GA and post-GA cleanup sections. The evidence does not give a GA release version.

The KEP's criteria for each stage:
- **Alpha:** API warnings, mandatory strict validation for `NetworkDeviceData`, kube-internal controllers writing only canonical IPs/CIDRs, and the validation available behind a disabled-by-default gate.
- **Beta:** the gate enabled by default. Beta could not happen until 3 releases had passed since Alpha. This ensured no components were still writing invalid values, and it matches the 1.33 → 1.36 timeline.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes tighten validation of IP addresses and CIDRs in API fields?
answer.answer:
Because the old validation was too lax: API fields accepted any string that Go's net.ParseIP / net.ParseCIDR accepted. Some of those strings were ambiguous and could cause security problems. Examples are IPv4 octets with leading 0s and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values such as ::ffff:192.168.0.1. The risk is that different components can read the same string as different IP addresses, as in CVE-2021-29923.

After Go 1.17 changed how it handles leading-zero IPs to address that CVE, there was consensus that Kubernetes API validation should become stricter too. This was not done right away because the project didn't want to retroactively invalidate existing API objects.

KEP-4858 sets out the plan:
- Several releases of apiserver warnings first.
- Then stricter validation behind the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate: alpha in 1.33, beta in 1.36.
- Existing invalid values do not have to be fixed on unrelated updates.

The goal is to make ambiguously interpretable IPs/CIDRs impossible going forward, at least in new clusters. The v1.36 release blog also says this helps catch malformed addresses that could lead to confusing runtime behavior or security surprises.

answer.question: How long does a Kubernetes minor release receive patch support?
answer.answer: Kubernetes 1.19 and newer receive approximately 1 year of patch support; 1.18 and older received about 9 months. The patch releases page puts the active support period at roughly 14 months. The first 12 months are the standard period. Toward the end of those 12 months, Release Managers cut a release and the series enters a two-month maintenance mode. During maintenance mode, extra releases may be cut only for CVEs, dependency issues (including base image updates) and critical core component issues. After that the series is end of life (EOL), and the 28th of the month is used as the target date for maintenance mode and EOL. The project maintains release branches for the three most recent minor releases.

answer.question: In which week of a Kubernetes release cycle does code freeze start?
answer.answer: It depends on the release. In current documentation (Kubernetes 1.24 onward, still valid now), Code Freeze starts in about week 12 and lasts roughly 2 weeks (weeks 12–14). The TL;DR sections of those releases describe the Code Freeze period as weeks 9–11. After Code Freeze there are about two weeks before release, during which remaining critical issues are resolved and documentation is finalized.

answer.question: When were the legacy apt.kubernetes.io and yum.kubernetes.io package repositories frozen, and when were they removed?
answer.answer:
The legacy Google-hosted repositories (apt.kubernetes.io and yum.kubernetes.io) were formally deprecated on August 31, 2023, and frozen on approximately September 13, 2023. The freeze came right after the September 2023 patch releases (v1.28.2, v1.27.6, v1.26.9, v1.25.14), which were the last to be published to both the legacy and the new pkgs.k8s.io repositories. From October 2023, packages were published only to pkgs.k8s.io.

The repositories were removed on March 4, 2024, and Kubernetes packages can no longer be installed from them. Earlier notices said they would go away in January 2024: the v1.29 release post said this, and an announcement on January 12, 2024 stated the intention to remove them that month. The removal actually happened on March 4, 2024.

heading_path: Why we decided to change the release cadence
What this means for end users

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes extend patch support for minor releases from 9 months to about a year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes extended patch support mainly in response to end-user requests. Business cycles such as financial, certification, sales, vacation and HR planning are overwhelmingly annual, so many users wanted at least a yearly support cycle. Nine months fit poorly with most companies' planning, operations and financial cycles. With a new minor release every three months, users also had to keep evaluating, planning and upgrading.

An early-2019 survey by WG LTS found that a large share of users did not upgrade within the 9-month window. About a third had production machines on versions already out of support. The survey suggested that a 12–14 month window would let those users stay on supported versions, raising the share on supported releases from about 50–60% to over 80%. This held for both DIY and vendor distributions.

The KEP saw the extension as a relatively small, viable change and a meaningful first response to users. Keeping it small would also help surface the unknowns of changing support windows.

The resulting policy is 14 months: roughly 12 months of standard support plus a 2-month maintenance and upgrade period. This formalized the existing practice of keeping patch-branch CI running 6–7 weeks past the 9 months. It applies starting with 1.19, which was planned as the first release to officially receive a year of patch support.

answer.question: How do I configure the kube-apiserver to use more than one authorization webhook?
answer.answer:
With the old command-line flags (`--authorization-*`, including `--authorization-modes`) you can enable only one webhook in the authorization chain. To use more than one, define the chain in a structured `AuthorizationConfiguration` file. That file lists the authorizers in order and lets each webhook have its own settings and failure behaviour.

How to set it up:
1. Write an `AuthorizationConfiguration` file (in the 1.30 blog examples: `apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1beta1`, `kind: AuthorizationConfiguration`).
2. Under `authorizers:`, list entries in the order they should be consulted. Each `type: Webhook` entry needs a unique `name` and a `webhook:` block. You can put `Node` and `RBAC` entries between or around the webhooks.
3. In each `webhook:` block, set:
   - `timeout` (required, max 30s)
   - `subjectAccessReviewVersion` (`v1` or `v1beta1`)
   - `matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion` (`v1`)
   - optional `authorizedTTL` and `unauthorizedTTL` cache durations
   - `failurePolicy`: `Deny` rejects the request without asking later authorizers; `NoOpinion` passes it on to the next authorizer
   - `connectionInfo`
4. Optionally add `matchConditions`: CEL expressions that decide which requests reach that webhook (at most 64). If any condition is false, the webhook is skipped. If all are true, it is called. If one errors, `failurePolicy` decides the outcome.

The `connectionInfo` type name differs by version:
- In the current (1.31+) version of the example it is `type: KubeConfigFile` plus `kubeConfigFile: <path>`.
- The 1.30-era version used `type: KubeConfig`.
- `InClusterConfig` is also listed as a type but is not allowed for kube-apiserver.

Example (current form):
```yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationConfiguration
authorizers:
  - type: Webhook
    name: system-crd-protector
    webhook:
      unauthorizedTTL: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      subjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      failurePolicy: Deny
      connectionInfo:
        type: KubeConfigFile
        kubeConfigFile: /files/kube-system-authz-webhook.yaml
      matchConditions:
      - expression: has(request.resourceAttributes)
  - type: Node
  - type: RBAC
  - name: opa
    type: Webhook
    webhook:
      unauthorizedTTL: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      subjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      failurePolicy: Deny
      connectionInfo:
        type: KubeConfigFile
        kubeConfigFile: /files/opa-default-authz-webhook.yaml
      matchConditions:
      - expression: has(request.resourceAttributes)
      - expression: request.resourceAttributes.namespace == 'default'
```

The evidence does not show the exact kube-apiserver flag used to point the server at this file.

answer.question: What were the graduation stages of KMS v2 encryption at rest?
answer.answer:
The KMSv2 feature gate (which enables the KMS v2 API for encryption at rest) went through these stages:
- Alpha in 1.25–1.26, disabled by default.
- Beta in 1.27–1.28, enabled by default.
- Stable (GA) from 1.29 through 1.31, enabled by default.

After that the gate was removed. The 1.32+ reference marks it `removed: true`.

The KEP-3299 criteria for each stage include:
- **Beta:** the feature is enabled by default, the documented tests are complete, there is documentation on building automatic-rotation components, a pkcs11 reference implementation exists, and there are performance metrics.
- **GA:** API server tracing for transformation timings, at least 2 KMSv2 plugin implementations, and a PKCS11 reference implementation.

KMS v1 was deprecated alongside this: deprecated but still on by default in 1.28, and disabled by default from 1.29.

heading_path: Migration from command line arguments to configuration file

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes add a structured authentication configuration file instead of keeping the --oidc-* flags?
answer.answer:
According to KEP-3331, structured config for OIDC authentication had been asked for in various contexts over several years. The project wanted to move away from a flag-based config that was "growing without bounds" to a proper versioned config format. That format would make it easier to support features users had requested:

- multiple client IDs
- identifying users by more than one JWT claim
- mapping any ID-token claim to user info extra attributes
- failing authentication unless the user belongs to specific groups
- array support in required claims
- forwarding audiences to authorization

The KEP's goals list the customizations the flags couldn't provide:

- **Claim validation rules:** the flags allowed only exact-value audience validation.
- **Claim mappings:** the flags allowed only one value from one claim, plus a group prefix; mappings would also cover nested claims.
- **Multiple OIDC providers:** otherwise you needed an external multiplexing provider.
- **No restarts:** authenticator settings could change without restarting kube-apiserver.
- **Validation on the final user info object:** so infra providers can safely expose this to customers.
- **Easy migration** from the existing OIDC flags.

The KEP also intends to drop `--oidc-signing-algs`, because all asymmetric algorithms will always be allowed. SIG Auth recommends the file-based approach because it offers more flexibility and extensibility.

The flags were not removed outright. The config file is backwards-compatible, and you can keep using the `--oidc-*` flags. However, `--authentication-config` is mutually exclusive with them: setting both makes the API server report an error and exit.

answer.question: Is kube-proxy's ipvs mode still supported, and what should I use instead?
answer.answer:
ipvs mode is still available, but it is deprecated. It was deprecated in v1.35, and kube-proxy now logs a warning on startup when you configure it to use ipvs.

The current plan is:
- **v1.37:** a `KubeProxyIPVS` feature gate was added, enabled by default.
- **v1.40:** ipvs mode is expected to be disabled by default. You can turn it back on with the `KubeProxyIPVS` feature gate.
- **v1.43:** ipvs mode is to be removed entirely.

The docs and the KEP give these reasons:
- The kernel IPVS API is a poor match for the Kubernetes Services API, and ipvs mode never handled every Service edge case correctly. It still uses iptables underneath.
- sig-network lacks maintainers familiar with the ipvs code.
- Supporting it alongside other modes added technical debt.

**What to use instead:** on Linux nodes, use the `nftables` proxy mode. It is the recommended replacement and performs better than both iptables and ipvs. If your Linux systems are too old for nftables, try `iptables` mode rather than ipvs, because iptables performance has improved a lot since ipvs was introduced.

To check which mode you are running:
`kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.conf}' | grep 'mode:'`

answer.question: Should a new controller watch Endpoints or EndpointSlices to find a Service's backends?
answer.answer:
Watch EndpointSlices, not Endpoints. As of Kubernetes 1.33 the v1 Endpoints API is officially deprecated, and the API server returns warnings to users who read or write Endpoints. Newer Service features are implemented only for EndpointSlice, including dual-stack, traffic distribution/topology, and Services with more than 1000 endpoints. For a dual-stack Service, the Endpoints object shows only the addresses in the cluster's primary address family. Service proxies, kube-proxy and Gateway API implementations have all moved to EndpointSlices. KEP-4974 plans to stop requiring the Endpoints controller for conformance, so clusters may run with it disabled, and then Endpoints objects might not exist at all.

When you consume EndpointSlices, keep in mind that a Service can have several of them. You find them with the label `kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>`. You will typically see multiple slices in three cases: a dual-stack Service has separate IPv4 and IPv6 slices; endpoints targeting different ports (for example during a rollout) go in separate slices; and a Service with more than 100 endpoints is split across slices.

heading_path: IPv4/IPv6 Dual-stack Networking graduates to GA
IPv4/IPv6 Dual-stack Networking graduates to GA

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20 dual-stack was not on by default. You turned it on by enabling the `IPv6DualStack` feature gate on the relevant components and setting dual-stack network assignments:

- **kube-apiserver:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`
- **kube-controller-manager:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`, `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`. The node CIDR mask size flags (`--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4` / `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6`) default to /24 for IPv4 and /64 for IPv6.
- **kubelet:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`
- **kube-proxy:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`

Example CIDRs are `10.244.0.0/16` for IPv4 and the format `fdXY:IJKL:MNOP:15::/64` for IPv6. In 1.20 dual-stack was reimplemented to support dual-stack Services. Once it was enabled, you could create Services using IPv4, IPv6, or both. It was still alpha in that release.

Later releases changed this: from 1.21 dual-stack was enabled by default, and in 1.23 the feature gate was removed.

answer.question: When did kube-proxy's nftables mode become generally available, and what came before?
answer.answer:
kube-proxy's nftables backend became stable (GA) in Kubernetes v1.33, where iptables still stays the default on Linux nodes for compatibility reasons.

It got there in two earlier steps:
- **Alpha (v1.29):** nftables mode was introduced as an alpha feature. At that point it was mostly the same as iptables mode in function, except that it does not support NodePorts on 127.0.0.1. It was not yet heavily optimized, and its nftables-specific settings could only be set through a config file.
- **Beta (v1.31):** it moved to beta behind the `NFTablesProxyMode` feature gate, which was enabled by default. It was Linux-only, required kernel 5.13 or later, and might not work with every network plugin. Some NodePort behaviors differed from iptables mode.

The KEP's implementation history lists these dates: initial proposal on 2023-02-01, merged on 2023-10-06, beta updates on 2024-05-24, and GA updates on 2025-01-15. A separate provisional KEP (KEP-5343) plans to make nftables the default proxy mode in a later release, which its GA section targets for 1.40.

heading_path: Were upgrade and rollback tested? Was the upgrade->downgrade->upgrade path tested?
Were upgrade and rollback tested? Was the upgrade->downgrade->upgrade path tested?

answer.question: How did support for multiple Service CIDRs (ServiceCIDR objects) progress through its release stages?
answer.answer:
Multiple Service CIDRs (KEP-1880), controlled by the MultiCIDRServiceAllocator feature gate, went through three stages:

- **Alpha, 1.27–1.30:** the gate was off by default.
- **Beta, 1.31–1.32:** the gate was still off by default. The beta graduation criteria were:
  - API stability, with ServiceCIDR immutability, a default IPFamily, and one or two IP families per ServiceCIDR.
  - Feedback from developers and users.
  - More complex testing scenarios.
  - Scale tests to O(10K) Services and O(1K) ranges.
  - O(1) allocation of a free address.
- **Stable (GA), 1.33 onward:** the gate is on by default and locked. The gate describes the feature as tracking Service cluster IP allocations with IPAddress objects.

The KEP's GA case cited:
- Real-world use in GKE since 1.31.
- Community testing since the 1.31 beta.
- Only one bug reported during beta.

An earlier version of the KEP planned a different rollout. It had the gate beta-on in 1.32, GA in 1.33, and a companion DisableAllocatorDualWrite gate. That gate would keep writing to both the old bitmap allocator and the new IPAddress objects during upgrades: alpha-off in 1.31–1.32, beta-off in 1.33, and GA-on in 1.34, when the old bitmap would be deleted. Both gates were planned for removal in 1.35. The feature gate reference, however, shows the beta default as false through 1.32.

answer.question: Why did SIG Network build a new nftables backend for kube-proxy?
answer.answer:
Several reasons are given. The iptables kernel subsystem has unfixable performance problems. Upstream development has moved from iptables to nftables: work on iptables has mostly stopped, and new features and performance improvements go mainly into nftables. Some Linux distributions had already started to deprecate and remove iptables, and nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems. The KEP also says that neither the ipvs mode nor the nf_tables mode of /sbin/iptables would solve these problems, and that the iptables mode of kube-proxy had grown crufty.

SIG Network was supporting both the iptables and ipvs backends. It felt it could not drop ipvs because of perceived iptables performance issues. A new backend as functional and non-buggy as iptables but as performant as ipvs could eventually let both existing backends be deprecated, leaving only one Linux backend to support. Writing a new mode was also expected to help focus cleanup and refactoring of the kube-proxy library code.
